title: The Growing Risk of Great Power War: A Conversation with Arne Westad
transcriptText:
Welcome to China Power. I'm Bonnie Lin,
[music] your host, and in this podcast,
we dissect critical issues underpinning
China as a global power.
>> [music]
>> Today, I am joined by Arne Westad, who
is an Elihu Professor of History at Yale
University.
Before joining Yale, he taught at the
London School of Economics, where he was
school professor of international
history, and at Harvard University,
where he was the ST Lee Professor of
US-Asia Relations. In this episode, we
will discuss his new book, The Coming
Storm: Power, Conflict, and Warnings
from History. Arne, thank you for
joining me.
>> It's great to be with you, Bonnie.
Always good to have a conversation.
>> Yes. Uh, so before we get to the book,
I'd like to ask you about your views on
recent US-China affairs and
developments. What has surprised you the
most in the past year? And this should
not be related to the findings in your
book.
>> So, I think what has surprised me the
most in US-China relations is the US war
with Iran.
Um, because it seems to me to move away
from so much of what this administration
had in mind with regard to its overall
international policy
um, since it came into into power. I I
was really surprised by it, not because
I believe that China in itself,
as some people in China
uh, indicating, I'm just back from from
Beijing. I was there last week. This was
directed against China,
but because of that
uh, redirection, that deflection from
what the administration had insisted
would be its laser-like focus focus on
East Asia and and and and on China. So,
that has been, I think, the biggest
surprise overall, that this
administration would move in the
direction of another
uh, Middle Eastern war that really has
a limited relevance I think with regard
to its overall rivalry with China.
>> But the US actions in Iran actually
relate to what you talk about in the
book. You mentioned that great powers
have been entangled in foreign wars.
You mentioned that both in terms of
Britain about a a century ago as well as
what we're seeing now in the United
States.
>> Yeah, that's true. I mean I think
unfortunately
this has made the book and what the book
tries to say even more relevant because
the the book is really about how
under circumstances of multipolarity
which I think we are in now and we were
in at the beginning of the 20th century.
That creates much more complexity,
much more diversity in terms of
international affairs. It makes it
harder to keep focus for the great
powers in terms of where their real
interests and preoccupations should be.
And I think we're seeing some of that
today as well. I mean especially perhaps
with the US war
against Iran. So
this is part of the message in the book
is that
these wars and conflicts that go off in
different directions and in different
regions
may under the worst case scenario have
an impact on overall great power
relations that could stimulate a
conflict and eventually a war
among them. So the book has a very clear
call to try to settle these kinds of of
regional conflicts, certainly not expand
them to intervention as we are seeing in
in Iran now. Not just because of the
effects of those actions by themselves,
but also because they threaten to make
great power relations much more
complicated overall.
>> And Arnie, one of the main purposes of
your book is to warn that great power
war is again possible. And and you just
highlighted some of the ways in which
there could be triggers or catalysts for
great power. But could you define or um
share like what exactly is a great power
war?
>> So, a great power war has to do with two
things. It has to do with the totality
of the war, I mean in terms of how it
spreads and and the dimension that it
has both both territorial and in terms
of intensity of conflict. And it also
has to do with what happens on the on
the battlefield. The number of people
who end up dead as a as a result of
great power war. So, as you know, in in
our world we have seen in our lives
we've seen
a great deal of conflict and a great
deal of wars and all of them are are
truly terrible.
But we've never experienced great power
war. We have to go back to the middle
part of the 20th century to see that.
And it's just 0.01%
of the population alive today who have
any experience with it. And those the
dimensions. And I remind the readers in
the book that if you use the First World
World War as an example, as I do,
in the Battle of the Somme in the summer
of 1916 during the First World War, uh
in the first two weeks of that battle as
many soldiers were killed as in all wars
between the end of the Napoleonic Wars
in 1815 and the outbreak of the First
World War. So, the point here is also in
terms of great power conflict about the
dimensions of it, about the the
significance of it in terms of
destruction.
>> Oh, well, that's a lot and that that
relates to your point of totality of how
much of the conflict is impacting not
only the regions in which we're seeing
conflict, but also those um the
countries involved. So, I think what in
in terms of the reference that you
mentioned in terms of the US-Iran
conflict right now, it really has very
limited impact so so on the United
States. And that is not what a great
power
great power war will be like.
>> Exactly. So, and this is I think the
part that people often get wrong.
So, all wars of course have terrible
impact, but
we have to be able to differentiate
in terms of scale and in terms of
totality.
And that's why we have to be very
careful with taking risks that could
lead us in the direction of great power
war. So, part of the argument in the
book, as you will have seen, is that
under those kinds of circumstances, what
we should try to do is not just reduce
overall tension among great powers, but
also reduce some of those immediate
causes for conflict. So, remember that
in that terrible summer of 1914, when
the world went from peace to war within
a very short period of time, a war that
no one expected at that moment.
It was one of those local conflicts, the
the the the conflict over Bosnia,
that set it in motion.
And these are the kinds of things that
we need to need to bear in mind, I
think, in our own time as well, that
it's really hard even for the world's
best best experts in government and
outside of government to foresee what
those flash points could be if tensions
among great powers are already running
very, very high and distrust is at a
at a at a very high level.
>> I do want to get to that, but maybe
before that, just to remind our
listeners, it would be useful to unpack
what actually happened right before
World War I. And you actually spent a
lot of your book not only talking about
history, but also talking about the
parallels between history and what we
have now.
So, you mention in your book that the
United States is like Britain of 100
years ago, China is like Germany, Russia
is today's Austria, India is today's
France. Could you
unpack a bit about what happened 100
years ago and why do these actors
resemble what we saw 100 years ago?
>> Well, we ought to be careful with all
these kinds of comparisons and and
parallels. None of them are exact.
But sometimes they help us think. So,
this book came about out of sheer
irritation with the use of the Cold War
parallel for our own time. And
>> [snorts]
>> as you know, I spent a lot of time
working on studying the Cold War as an
international system and its various
incarnations. And I see very little in
the world that we are living in today
that reminds me of how the Cold War
worked. It's not bipolar, you know, it
it happens within the same economic
system, broadly speaking. It's not
driven driven by narrow-minded concepts
of ideology, et cetera, et cetera. So,
it seems to me that if you want to use
historical parallels, we'll have to find
something that fits the terrain a little
bit better.
And unfortunately, it seems to me that
the late 19th century and the early 20th
century, the period before the First
World War, is much better suited for us
to try to make some sense of what is
happening today. Like our own time, it
was it was multipolar. The leading
power, which back then was Britain,
today the United States,
was in many ways in retreat or had
decided itself that it wasn't really
benefiting from the global economic
system that it had set up
uh the first wave of globalization in
the in the 19th century and then started
retreating for it from it at the same
time as you had powerful new rising
powers, back then Germany and the United
States,
challenging that international system
overall. So, it was a pretty combustible
kind of setting, similar to what we have
today. So,
the reason why I use Germany as a
parallel uh to China is that Germany
came out of nothing in the late 19th
century and grew to become the most
significant power in what was then the
most important part of the world, which
was Europe. Just like China has done
over the past generation within what is
today, in my view, the most important
part of the world in in Eastern Asia.
So, these are the kinds of parallels
that I'm looking for in the book. They
cannot be absolute. Um and I think all
of them have, you know, there are there
are differences in terms of what
happened back then what's happening
today. But these kinds of
parallels, these kinds of of similes in
a way with regard to what happened in
the past, sometimes under the best kind
of circumstance will help us think. And
that's what I'm trying to to to get us
to do through this book.
>> I found your parallel of um between the
United States and Britain to be very
very uncanny, even as you write in the
book. Um it it it wasn't just at the
parallels in terms of the how Britain
was in in the international order, but
the policies between President Trump and
what was happening then in Britain. Um
but as we look at uh
in focusing particularly on the United
States and China, what about the
dynamics from 100 years ago that worry
you the most when you look at current
US-China relations?
>> Well, I think there are two things first
and foremost. I mean, one is the rise in
mutual distrust
and this general conflation of issues or
challenges
that come together
in the foreign policy of both countries.
So, with everything that happens
in one country that goes against the
interests of its government is ascribed
to the other power, right? That was
exactly what the relationship between
Britain and Um, and Germany was like
before the First World War.
And very similar to what you see today
in the relationship between China and
the United States.
It's all because of China.
One often hears in the United States.
It's all It's always because of the
United States you hear in China. So,
that that's the first similarity.
The second one
is with regard to very unclear policies
in terms of what the two countries want
to achieve.
I think part of the real problem that
Germany had before the First World War
was that it wasn't able to define
what it wanted of the international
system except, you know, more for
Germany. It wanted more for
uh the German position overall with
regard to international affairs,
with regard to trade relations, with
regard to
um global influence, but it wasn't
entirely sure how it wanted to set that
up and what the direction was.
And a little bit similar in terms of the
relationship between Britain and the
United States.
Both knew that they wanted to get more
from for themselves out of the
international system that they had been
the central power in creating.
But they weren't quite certain how to do
that and often overreacted with regard
to international issues, right? Um,
Britain, like the United States today,
was deflected from
what I would regard as its core
purposes, which would be to offer some
kind of believable deterrence against
war in Europe, by different kinds of
colonial wars that really mattered very
little in terms of the overall
constellation of power. A little bit
like the United States now is drawn into
areas in which US strategic purpose is
actually quite limited. So, those are
some of the similarities. There are more
of them, unfortunately, Bonnie, but but
those are the main similarities that I
see.
>> And your book also talks about the
different uh alliance relationships as
well as uh Britain's willingness or I
guess hesitation in terms of committing
to other countries. Could you talk about
how that also plays a role?
>> So, very often the story that we hear
about the First World War is that it
came about because of alliances and
alliance entanglements.
I think a lot of historians, myself
included, would regard that as being
untrue.
It came about because of alliances that
did not work or at least did not work
the way they were supposed to work,
which is to have a deterrent
a deterrent role with regard to the
oncoming of great power wars. It was all
of those uncertainties that had been
created in the alliance systems prior to
World War I, which, in my view, were
crucial in terms of how the war broke
out. Um there wasn't enough believable
deterrence to use those kinds of those
kinds of concepts. And that turned out
to be very dangerous
uh when a real world-class crisis came
along as it did in the summer of 1914,
almost out of nothing. Uh a terrorist
act,
uh the the murder of um the heir to the
Austrian throne
in Sarajevo. Um you know, the
the fact that there wasn't enough
deterrent power
in those alliances. No one knew, for
instance, what Britain was going to do.
Uh and and I'm among those who believe
that if Germany hadn't had basically
just one military strategy, which was to
try to knock out France by invading
neutral Belgium, uh Britain might very
well have stayed out of this war, right?
So, this made the calculations so much
more difficult among people who were
already very fearful, almost panicky, in
the summer of 1914 because they couldn't
easily foresee what kind of consequences
their actions would have.
>> And part of your book talks about um
what are some of the current catalysts
for great power conflict between the
United States and China, but also within
among the other other powers, too.
Could you describe a bit more about how
Taiwan from your perspective resembles
what we saw in 1914?
>> Unfortunately, Taiwan is a little bit I
think I say this in the book.
It's a little bit like Bosnia,
Alsace and Belgium rolled into one. So,
it has the same
um nationalist implications as Bosnia,
this intensity of of nationalist feeling
on on on both sides
that led to conflict in 1914. It has the
territorial implications of
Alsace-Lorraine, which France and
Germany had been in conflict over for a
very, very long time.
And it has the strategic implications of
Belgium in the sense that
about the only thing that Germany could
do in the summer of 1914 that would
guarantee that this would become a world
war by pulling in the United Kingdom was
invading Belgium, which was the only
European country that
um that Britain had a treaty agreement
with.
So,
that's how I see the similarity with
Taiwan. Taiwan has all of these
dimensions, you know, in terms of the
overall framework. What I'm saying with
regard to Taiwan, and it's very
important not to be misunderstood on
this, I'm not calling for uh you know,
the United States to abandon
its policy with regard to Taiwan of a
level of of strategic ambiguity.
What I am saying is that it's very
important under those circumstances not
to give China the impression
that the US commitment to Taiwan to to
support Taiwan, to uphold
Taiwan
um is flagging, because that's one of
the things that really went wrong in in
1914 It basically that the challenges,
great power challenges, thought that the
key power
Britain back then had weakened to the
point that they actually could carry out
stuff that they couldn't carry out or or
at least couldn't carry out except
through through through global war. So
I'm, you know, in the book I'm
discussing both the short-term
perspective with regard to Taiwan, which
is one
has to be one of status quo.
And the long-term perspective where I'm
among those who are more in favor of
some kind of
at least
if not settlement of of abatement of the
overall conflict through negotiations
between Taiwan and the mainland. And
longer term, when the political
circumstances in both places would allow
for it to set up some kind of of
agreement or even possibly some kind of
broad confederation.
that would enable the core issue of
conflict, if not to go away, at least to
be to be significantly reduced. But we
are not there now. Um you know
this is the I've just been
talking about this in Beijing.
I mean on the Chinese side, just like
what was the case with Germany before
World War I. So Germany grew up to today
to to become the most significant power
in Europe, but it happened, you know,
to result in two world wars and a global
depression and a cold war and all of all
of that. China doesn't want to do that,
right? China wants to grow naturally,
regionally in terms of economic power
and for that matter military power into
a position where it at some point does
become the predominant power within the
the wider East Asian region and possibly
um then moving towards some kind of
unification with Taiwan as well.
But it's the timing of that that
actually matters. If one tries to push
that process too much
then, you know, the cataclysms that
could come out of that are quite visible
if you use the early 20th century as a
mirror.
>> Um given [clears throat] your recent
travel to China, did you get a sense um
from your Chinese interlocutors and
colleagues
that they sense that US commitment to
Taiwan is weakening and that there might
be more opportunity for them to take
various types of actions?
>> Yes.
>> Basically what you outlined in what
happened in 1914.
>> Yes. I think
I think both in terms of
US commitments
overall, but also in the relative
constellation of power, and perhaps most
crucially
um the development on the island itself.
I mean, this is the thing that really
worries me.
Is the number of people, otherwise
sensible people, in Beijing who are now
saying that time for achieving
unification is running out.
And they're not saying that, and I think
it's very important for our for our
listeners to to to get that. They're not
saying it mainly because of changes in
the in the military, you know, overall
military constellations. They are saying
it because of the feeling that many
positions decision makers on the
mainland have that in another
generation, maybe even another half
generation, the people of Taiwan are not
going to feel Chinese anymore.
I mean, one of them was saying to me,
"This is our real challenge, I mean,
from a from a mainland perspective, that
even if you are able to take over the
island, govern the island, it would then
take us a very very long time to be able
to work with people's minds so that they
get, you know, a sense of of actually
being Chinese, of belonging to the same
nation."
And
that kind of thinking worries me because
that also brings us in brings us back to
the German situation before World War I
where I think Germany's willingness to
take risks when this
global crisis came along in the summer
of 1914 which was not a crisis that
Germany itself had provoked. It was its
ally Austria that that that that set
this up.
you know, there was a willingness to
take risks because there was an
uncertainty whether Germany would have
better opportunities to achieve what it
wanted to do in Europe later.
What some people call the maximum moment
kind of idea.
And I'm not saying that China is quite
there yet, but I do worry about this and
and I think it's very very important
that
leaders in Beijing
do not move into the illusion that this
is something
uh in terms of
taking military action against Taiwan
that this is something that would be
preferable to other courses of action.
>> And aren't you you you already started
talking about this. As you mentioned
also in the book, the important roles
that both fear and misperception played
in 1940 as well as um the role that
technology played in shortening the time
to think through and make decisions.
Could you unpack all three factors and
the role that they played a century ago
and how you see that right now in
US-China relations?
>> So what what you're right. One of the
most striking similarities Bonnie with
with uh the world before 1914 and the
world today is that we've gone through
very significant, very rapid
technological transformations
which have led to the sense of speed of
action and and thereby necessarily the
speed of decision-making
just becoming much much higher. The the
the the the timing for this
uh has sped up and I think there is a a
direct connection
between that and and what went wrong
in 1914, which was this onset of
an almost debilitating fear
in late July
1914 with regard to being too late or
not acting offensively quickly enough
and thereby leaving the advantages to
one's opponents.
And I think
the coming together
of those kinds of thinking, so
previously existing fears and
resentments
and in part through technology and
military strategy, that sense at a
particular point in time that one had to
act very very quickly in order not to be
disadvantaged.
I think
that's a parallel that I can see easily
with our own time as well. And that I
really really worry about.
>> And in addition to Taiwan, your book
also talks about other scenarios or
potential flashpoints that could bring
the great powers to war.
Um so I think Taiwan was top of your
list, but you also had scenarios
involving North Korea, uh
in Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and
India. Could Could you talk through sort
what you had in mind for those and what
worried you the most of those scenarios?
>> Well, the problem in a way Bonnie is
that there isn't
you know, any shortage of these kinds of
conflicts in today's world. In a way
there are many more of them even than
existed in the early 20th century that
could lead under the worst-case
circumstances to a bigger conflagration.
But if we if we just think about Eastern
Asia
I think the relationship um with regard
to the Korean Peninsula is one of those
that worried me most because it is one
of those that
no great power really has any kind of
total control over, right? In in terms
of what what happens in the north when
that regime goes so get into even more
serious trouble than it is in today. And
I think that unpredictability and lack
of discussion, lack of conversation,
even lack of understanding in a
strategic sense that exists between the
United States and and China and for that
matter United States China Japan Russia
with regard to the the Korean Peninsula
is is one of my biggest worries. I could
easily see in today's situation that if
anything serious were to happen on the
Korean Peninsula, it would be really
very very hard to keep the great powers
out of that and first and foremost the
United States and
and China because so many would see that
as an immediate and very acute threat.
I also talked a great deal in the book
about India. Because India in many ways
is the most striking among the rising
great powers of our time. Uh it has a
great deal of
of of development still to undertake and
probably within the next generation, it
will still be quite far behind the
United States and China.
But it's still making its own strategic
decisions and calculations with regard
to its position. And of course one of
those that's very very clear is the
sense that China is out to dominate
India, that it's out to put pressure on
India both through the conflict in the
Himalayas and through the Chinese
uh alliance with with with Pakistan.
And that's why I say the book slightly
tongue-in-cheek that that India is a
little bit like France. I mean, what I
mean by that uh is that France before
the First World War was had territorial
conflicts as we already talked about,
with uh uh with Germany.
But it also had this sense
that Germany's policy was directed
against France in all respects, right?
That it was out to dominate France. That
it was out to
to take advantage of of France.
And when I visit India, I often get a
little bit of that impression with
regard to in India's views of China
today.
When you're in Beijing, you don't hear
about India all that often. You hear
about it increasingly and from time to
time.
But in Delhi, you hear a great deal
about China.
>> So, I do want to get to your
recommendations of how to change this
trajectory that we're we might be on
that your book warns about, but before
that I want to also go back to a point
that you made earlier, but I think it's
really important to emphasize, which is
that you mentioned that no one expected
in 1941 that a great power war or war or
a world war would break out. But it's a
variety of factors that you mentioned,
the miscalculations from multipolarity,
the
um how the alliances didn't quite work
that they the way that they did, the
fears, the fast pace of technology. A
lot of these factors added together that
that contribute to a small
um spark lead leading to um a
a much more uh a variety of cascading
actions. Is there anything you want to
add there in terms of why it's so
difficult to predict and we might it
might not be useful for us to predict
what might lead to the next conflict,
but just understanding that once we have
all these dynamics in place, any of
these potential scenarios might be a
a catalyst or one of multiple catalysts?
>> So, I think the most important part of
this is that there are lots of people in
our time, just like there were in the
early 20th century, who say that great
power war just cannot happen. All right,
the the existence of weapons of mass
destruction, the
understanding of interests in a sort of
broader global
global sense.
Um the lessons that we have drawn
through the disasters of the 20th
century, all of that points away from a
great power war in our time. And what
what frightens me about that, Bonnie, is
that that's almost exactly what people
said in the early 20th century before
1914. There were
best sellers written
just a few months before war broke out
explaining in in great detail why under
these circumstances, for instance, the
new kinds of destructive technology that
had come up um
aerial bombardments,
battleships, long-distance artillery,
poison gas. Under these kinds of
circumstances, great power war, it was
all good, were next to
unthinkable.
And we of course have some of that. We
see some of that same
complacency today that people just do
not think based on the long period of
great power peace that we had since the
end of the Second World War, that
something like this could happen again.
Um and that's my big worry. Not because
I'm certain that it's going to happen.
I think we have a very decent chance of
avoiding it. But we can't avoiding it
avoid it through complacency. We can
only avoid it if we try try to think
about ways in which we can act on all
sides to reduce the the possibility for
this actually happen happening rather
than believing that it's circumstance
that leads us away from it. And one of
those circumstances, of course, being
a realization of just how destructive
these kinds of wars are. Unfortunately,
in the past, all through human history,
not just in the early 20th century, we
find that those kinds
of beliefs are not strong enough when a
real crisis comes along and tensions are
already running high to avoid the
ultimate disaster.
>> And all the new technologies are in that
you mentioned in 1914, they were all
used in the war afterwards,
unfortunately. So now let's move to I
guess one of the most important parts of
your book, which is your recommendations
of what we should be doing now. You've
already alluded to some of that earlier
in terms of um
you mentioned earlier the need to reduce
between great powers, but your book also
has some other specific recommendations
or at least urgent steps that we should
take. Um could you share with them what
they are and from your perspective, what
are some of the most immediate steps
that we should be taking?
>> I think the most important thing at the
moment is to try to improve the kind of
communications that we have among top
leaders. I know just them getting
together and meeting each other. I mean
that happened a great deal before 1914
as well.
We must never forget that uh in three of
the
what became the warring states, Russia,
Germany and and Britain their heads of
state were cousins. They knew each other
really really well, right? Um Tsar
Nicholas
uh Kaiser Wilhelm
and the British King George.
so it's it's more of
>> [clears throat]
>> it's about the understanding of each
others um
strategic priorities.
What could lead to war in the eyes of of
other powers? And try to think through
those kinds of scenarios. That is what
is really needed, I think, and and in
the upcoming um
summit as we hope it will be between
President Xi and President Trump, these
are the kinds of issues uh that need to
be need to be dealt with. Not just the
surface issues, but a a better
understanding of where the other power
wants to go. So I think that's the first
that's the first part.
The second part is that we need to
revive, particularly under the
circumstances of multipolarity, some of
the international institutions that were
set up in the 20th century to avoid
great power war. First and foremost, the
United Nations,
which needs to be reformed, but also to
be drawn on, be be used for purposes of
of greater stability.
I also think we need to look much more
seriously at arms control. I mean, one
of the things that really frightens me
compared to the situation that led to
the war in 1914,
is that we now seem to have learned very
